title: How to read a crochet chart
subtitle: The symbols, and how the picture is put together
excerpt: A crochet chart draws the pattern as a picture made of stitch symbols, instead of writing it out in words. Once you know a few symbols and which way to read them, a chart shows the shape of a piece at a glance. This explains the symbols our charts use and how to follow them.
sourceNotes: Symbol set described here matches the international crochet symbol convention used by the Homemade chart engine, which follows the same standard as common modern pattern books. The historical practice of charting crochet on a squared grid is documented in Victorian needlework manuals including Weldon's Practical Needlework and Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886). All public domain; the text here is our own.

glossaryTerms.definition: A drawing of a crochet pattern that uses a small symbol for each stitch, laid out in the shape of the finished piece, so you can see the structure at a glance.
The small panel beside a chart that lists each symbol and the stitch it stands for, so you can decode the drawing.

content.text: What a crochet chart is
A
crochet chart

draws a pattern as a picture instead of writing it out in words. Each stitch gets a small symbol, and the symbols are arranged in the shape of the finished piece. A round motif is charted as a set of rings; a flat piece is charted as a grid of rows. The chart shows the structure at a glance, which is often easier to follow than a long block of abbreviations, especially for motifs.
Charts and written patterns say the same thing two ways. Many patterns give both, so you can read whichever suits you and use one to check the other when you lose your place.
The symbols
The symbols follow a shared international convention, so a chart from one book reads much like a chart from another. The ones our charts use most are these:
An open oval is a chain.
A small filled dot is a slip stitch.
A cross or plus sign is a double crochet.
An upright line with one bar across it is a treble. More bars mean a taller stitch: two bars for a double treble, three for a triple treble.
Several tall stitches joined at the base in a fan shape make a shell; several joined at the top make a cluster or bobble.
Every chart carries a
legend
that lists the symbols it uses, so you never have to guess. Read the legend first.
How to read the chart

For a motif worked in the round, start at the centre and read outward, one ring per round, in the direction the round is worked. For a flat piece worked in rows, start at the bottom. Read right-side rows from right to left, and wrong-side rows from left to right, because the work is turned at the end of each row. Row numbers run up the side of the chart to keep your place.

The chart shows where each stitch sits in relation to the ones below it, so you can see, for example, that a cluster is worked into a chain space rather than into a stitch. That spatial information is the chart's strength: it makes the shape of the pattern obvious in a way a written list cannot.
Where to start

Pick a simple charted motif, such as a granny square, and follow the chart and the written pattern side by side for the first round or two. Once you can match the symbols to the stitches your hands already know, the chart becomes the faster way to read. The stitch tutorials in this section name each symbol as it teaches the stitch, so you can build the vocabulary one stitch at a time.
